name: Countess Lacroix

inspiration.oldScript: The queer-coded seducer vampire who preys on boys next door, from Dracula to Fright Night.
inspiration.newLens: A disco diva clinging to her golden age. The bite is nostalgia, and the Best ending lets her finally, gorgeously age.

logline: Club Lacroix closed in 1980, but under the Glitter Box dance floor the Countess is still throwing the party of the century. Dance under her mirror ball and she takes a little of your youth with every song.
backstory: She told everyone she was a countess from the Carpathians. She was Doreen Mudge from Modesto, a bit actress who started out in 1950s B movies until the studios fired her at twenty-five for being too old to play the girl. So she moved to Glimmer Falls, bought the shuttered old Rialto theatre and turned it into Club Lacroix, the only disco in a hundred miles where the mirror ball shone on everybody: farm kids, drag queens, shy boys in borrowed platforms, anyone who needed one night to be fabulous. Her motto was painted over the bar: EVERYBODY IS SOMEBODY UNDER THE BALL. On New Year's Eve 1977, terrified of turning forty at midnight, she let a mysterious guest who called himself the Baron kiss her on the neck in exchange for forever. It worked, and the world aged without her anyway. Disco died. A KGLM shock jock blew up a crate of disco records at the high school stadium. Her regulars got mortgages and reading glasses, and she turned them away at her own velvet rope for being bad for the look. In 1980 she locked the doors, lifted the needle off the last song before it could end, and sealed herself in a mirrored coffin under the dance floor. A year later a drag queen named Glory bought the building for a dollar and made it the Glitter Box. Now the Heartstone has woken the Countess, platform boots first, and she is hungry for the one thing she never had enough of.

centralIssue.title: Clinging to youth and a lost golden age
centralIssue.summary: The Countess believes getting older means disappearing, because the first world she loved told her so at twenty-five. She drains the young to stay forever 1977, but what she really lost was not her youth; it was the people she pushed away for aging. Learn who told her she had an expiration date, what she did to her own regulars, and why she never let the last song end, and show her that growing older can be fabulous.

poster: A glamorous vampire disco diva in a white jumpsuit with a towering collar and a black satin cape, a lion's mane of golden hair, fangs glinting, arms raised beneath a giant glowing mirror ball over a crowded dance floor, teenage dancers below graying and slumping in cardigans as golden light streams from them up into the ball
portrait: Close portrait of a camp 1970s vampire countess with sky-high feathered golden hair, glitter eyeshadow, wine-dark lipstick over two delicate fangs, a rhinestone choker, a single silver strand of hair she is pretending to ignore, lit by spinning mirror ball sparkles
endingPhoto: A glamorous vampire disco diva in a white jumpsuit and black satin cape gliding down a light-up dance floor staircase, golden lion's-mane hair and gleaming fangs, a giant mirror ball scattering moonlight, dancers in glitter hypnotized mid-hustle, teens with garlic necklaces and a mirror sneaking along the bar behind her
taunts: Darling, nobody ages on my dance floor. Nobody leaves it, either.
Gray is a color for pigeons.
Hustle, sweetie. Hustle until you drop.
It's always 1977 somewhere, and that somewhere is me.

clues.title: The last page of the guest book
clues.hint: The Glitter Box was a disco before it was a playhouse. The stage manager has found a trapdoor nobody remembers building.

encounter.title: Under the Stage
encounter.place: Beneath the stage, The Glitter Box Playhouse
encounter.text: Frankie Fontaine is flat on her stomach on the stage with a flashlight in her teeth, prying at a square of floorboards that sparkle when the light hits them. "Glitter in the grout," she says. "Real glitter, under five years of stage paint. This was a dance floor." Below it, a ladder leads down into a mirrored DJ booth, cobwebs strung with sequins, and a white leather guest book still open on the console.
encounter.art: A 24-year-old trans woman stage manager with long dark curls in a high side ponytail, a pencil through it, a black headset and a cropped black crew jacket lying flat on a theater stage with a flashlight in her teeth, prying up a square of floorboards that sparkle with glitter, below the opening a ladder down into a mirrored 1970s DJ booth with cobwebs strung with sequins and a white leather guest book lying open on the console, a teenager kneeling beside her, flashlight beam and dim stage light, high angle shot

choices.label: Help Frankie get the trapdoor open and climb down first

success.text: The guest book is a love letter to a nightclub. Hundreds of signatures from 1976: Best night of my life! First time I danced with a boy! Gloria, age 34, I felt like a STAR. Then the pages thin. By 1980 there is only one hand: July 4. Found a gray hair. ONE. The Baron swore. Told Sal and Gloria not to come back, the regulars are getting old and it shows. If I can't stay young, I'll stay 1977.
success.art: A teenager in a mirrored underground DJ booth reading a white leather guest book by flashlight, the early pages crowded with joyful signatures, the last page a single lonely entry in looping script

failure.text: The trapdoor drops open and the turntable below starts spinning by itself. A woman's laugh, husky and delighted, rises out of the dark with a blast of cold air and perfume. Frankie slams the trapdoor and sits on it. "Nope. We are calling Glory first."
failure.art: A trap door on a stage slamming shut on a blast of cold glittering air, a stage manager sitting on it firmly, a teen staggering back, faint disco light leaking through the cracks

choices.label: Ask Glory who Gloria, age 34, might be

success.text: Glory turns the guest book page and touches her own signature like an old photograph. "I hosted her Thursday nights. She was the first person who ever paid me to be fabulous." Her voice goes quiet. "Then one night, at her own rope, she looked at my crow's feet and said I was bad for the look. I bought this building to prove her wrong. I didn't know she was still under it."
success.alone: Nobody's free to ask, but the guest book answers for itself: Gloria, age 34, hostess, Thursdays, signed in the same purple ink as every Glitter Box flyer. Beside it, in a sharp hand: Bad for the look. Crow's feet. Struck from the rope. Whoever bought this building years later was proving somebody wrong, and never knew that somebody was still under it.
success.art: A drag queen in a sequined robe at a backstage vanity holding an old white leather guest book, touching a signature with a long painted nail, bittersweet expression, bulb lights glowing

failure.text: Glory is gluing on lashes ten minutes to curtain and has no time for ghosts. "Later, baby." As you leave, her vanity mirror fogs, and in the fog a woman in a white jumpsuit blows you a kiss with two very sharp teeth.
failure.alone: Backstage is a stampede ten minutes to curtain, and nobody has time for ghosts. As you leave, a vanity mirror fogs, and in the fog a woman in a white jumpsuit blows you a kiss with two very sharp teeth.
failure.art: A fogged backstage vanity mirror showing a glamorous woman in a white jumpsuit blowing a kiss with tiny fangs, a drag queen gluing on lashes oblivious

clues.title: Bat Bride Number Three
clues.hint: The woman at the Rewind Video counter was a 1950s scream queen. Ask her who played the third bat bride.

encounter.title: Attack of the Bat Brides
encounter.text: Zelda Fishbein is rewinding returns at the counter when you mention Club Lacroix. She stops the tape with one long red nail. "Oh, honey. Doreen." She pulls a dusty clamshell from under the counter: ATTACK OF THE BAT BRIDES, 1956. On the cover a young Zelda screams in a negligee, and behind her, third bat from the left, a blonde with very familiar cheekbones.
encounter.art: A 63-year-old woman with a silver-streaked black bouffant, cat-eye glasses on a pearl chain, bright red lipstick, long red nails and a red video-store vest standing at a rental counter holding up a dusty clamshell videotape case painted with screaming 1950s starlets and women with bat wings, shelves of horror tapes behind her, a teenager leaning on the counter, warm fluorescent store light, medium shot

choices.label: Ask Zelda how she knew Doreen

success.text: "She was my roommate on Gower Street, eighteen years old, with a hot plate and a cat." Zelda smiles. "At twenty-five the studio told her she was too old to play the girl. They told me the same thing ten years before. I decided to rot gracefully, and I'm having a ball. Doreen decided she would never rot at all." She taps the cover. "She was a terrible actress and the best friend I ever had. Tell her Zelda says her roots are showing."
success.art: An older former scream queen laughing behind a video store counter, holding a 1950s publicity photo of two young actresses arm in arm, a teen listening

failure.text: Zelda waves the tape at you. "Rent it like everybody else. Two-night rental, a dollar fifty." When you check it out, the clamshell is ice cold, and the bat bride on the cover has turned her head to look at you.
failure.art: A VHS clamshell on a video store counter with one bat bride on the cover turned to stare out at the viewer, frost forming at the edges

choices.label: Watch the movie on the back-room TV and look for Doreen

success.text: Bat Bride Number Three gets one line: "The night is young, and so am I." You rewind it four times. On the fifth, the tape skips to something that was never in the movie: a young blonde crying in a dressing room while a man in a suit tells her she has "an expiration date, like milk." Then the tape goes back to bats.
success.art: A teenager in a cramped video store back room watching a flickering TV showing a black and white scene of a young actress crying in a dressing room while a studio executive lectures her

failure.text: The tape eats itself halfway through, spewing ribbon across the floor, and the TV static forms a face with very shiny teeth. "Be kind, rewind," it purrs. The back room lights pop, one after another, and you leave owing Zelda a late fee and a lightbulb.
failure.art: A VCR spewing tangled tape ribbon in a dark video store back room, a TV screen of static forming a fanged smiling face, lightbulbs popping overhead

clues.title: The song that never ended
clues.hint: Tuesday is Disco Night at the roller-rink annex behind Pump Iron. The rink manager used to be somebody's dance partner.

encounter.title: Disco Tuesday
encounter.place: The roller-rink annex, Pump Iron Gym
encounter.text: Disco Night at the rink draws exactly four regulars, all over fifty, and they are having more fun than anyone you have ever seen. The best of them is Sal Gennaro, the rink manager, a barrel-chested man with a silver pompadour skating backward in a satin jacket, spinning, hands in the air. When he sees the Club Lacroix matchbook in your hand, he coasts to a stop.
encounter.art: A small roller rink at night under colored spotlights, four joyful skaters over fifty in satin jackets, a barrel-chested man with a silver pompadour skating backward with both hands in the air, a teenager standing at the rail holding a small vintage nightclub matchbook, a mirror ball scattering white dots, pink and gold rink light, wide shot

choices.label: Ask Sal for the couples skate and talk while you roll

success.text: Sal steers you around the rink like a pro. "Doreen and me won the Glimmer Falls Hustle Championship three years running." He spins you. "When the regulars got old, she shut us out. Said we were bad for the look. Last night the club was open, she was playing our song, Night Fever Forever. She lifted the needle before it could end. Couldn't stand to let anything finish." He presses a scratched record into your hands. "I've kept it. Somebody should let it end."
success.art: A teenager and a silver-haired older man couples-skating under colored rink lights, the man mid-spin, a scratched disco record tucked under his arm

failure.text: Your skates go out from under you on the first turn and you take Sal down with you. He laughs it off, but by the time you are both up, the lights flicker and the rink speakers start playing a song with no ending, the same chorus, over and over. Sal goes pale and shuts the rink early.
failure.art: A teenager and an older man sprawled on a roller rink floor, the colored lights flickering, a rink speaker glowing as a looping record plays

choices.label: Slip into the rink's record booth and dig through Sal's crates

success.text: In a crate labeled CLUB L, LAST NIGHT, is one record with a deep scratch three minutes in, as if a needle had been dragged off it in a hurry. Taped to the sleeve, in Sal's handwriting: She never let it end. July 4, 1980. Under that, newer, in pencil: Doreen, if you ever come back, I'll still skate with you. Gray hair and all.
success.art: A cramped roller rink DJ booth with crates of records, a teenager holding a disco single with a deep scratch and a handwritten note taped to its sleeve

failure.text: The booth door swings shut behind you. Every record in the crates starts spinning in its sleeve with a dry whisper, and in the booth window, reflected but not behind you, a woman in a cape is tapping her platform boot, waiting for you to dance.
failure.art: A dark rink DJ booth with records spinning in their sleeves, a booth window reflecting a vampire diva in a cape tapping her platform boot behind a frightened teen

signature.title: The Velvet Rope
signature.place: A back alley off Main Street, midnight
signature.text: A door that was not there yesterday glows red in the alley behind the Glitter Box. A velvet rope, a bouncer with leathery wings folded under his tuxedo, and a sign in gold script: CLUB LACROIX, TONIGHT ONLY, FOREVER 1977. A line of kids from school snakes down the block. As you watch, a sophomore stumbles out the exit in a cardigan, rubbing her lower back, complaining about property taxes.
signature.art: A dark alley behind a small-town theater at midnight, a door glowing deep red where a brick wall should be, a velvet rope on brass posts, a bouncer in a tuxedo with leathery bat wings folded behind his back, a line of high school kids in jackets waiting along the wall, a dazed teenage girl stumbling out of the exit in a frumpy beige cardigan rubbing her lower back, red door light and blue shadows, wide shot

choices.label: Sweet-talk the bouncer and get inside to pull the kids out

success.text: You tell the bat-bouncer you are on the list as "the Hustle Champion of 1978," and he is so impressed with your nerve that he unhooks the rope. Inside, you grab hands and yank kids off the dance floor one by one, out the back door, still young, still giggling. Their youth sticks to them like glitter.
success.art: A teen leading a chain of dancing teenagers out the back of a glittering disco club by the hands, a bat-winged bouncer looking impressed at the velvet rope

failure.text: The bouncer looks you up and down. "Not tonight, sweetheart. Shoes." When you push past anyway, the music hits you like a wave of warm syrup, and you dance two songs before you can stop. You walk out with your knees aching and an inexplicable urge to watch the evening news.
failure.art: A teen stumbling out of a glowing club exit with a hand on their aching knee, holding a newspaper they cannot remember picking up, a bouncer smirking

choices.label: Find the alley fire alarm and empty the club

success.text: The alarm bell screams and the sprinklers kick on inside. Kids pour out of the door shrieking and laughing, soaked, hair flattened, young as ever. From somewhere deep in the club a woman's voice howls, "My HAIR!" and the glowing door snaps shut like a compact.
success.art: Soaked laughing teens pouring out of a nightclub door into an alley as sprinklers spray inside, a fire alarm bell ringing on the brick wall

failure.text: The alarm handle comes off in your hand. Glitter, not water, sprays from the sprinklers inside, and the kids dance harder. A cold hand with very long nails rests on your shoulder. "You're cute. Come back when you're ready to dance."
failure.art: A teenager holding a broken fire alarm handle in an alley, glitter spraying from inside a club doorway, a long-nailed hand resting on their shoulder from behind

signature.title: Moonlight Roller Boogie
signature.place: The roller-rink annex, Pump Iron Gym, after hours
signature.text: The rink lights are off but the mirror ball is spinning. The Countess glides out of the dark on white roller skates, cape snapping, followed by her backup dancers, the Lacroix Lovelies, four pale skaters in matching gold hot pants with bat-wing capes. "A little race, darling," she purrs. "Ten laps. You win, the kids go home. I win, I keep your twenties."
signature.art: A dark roller rink after hours lit only by a spinning mirror ball, a glamorous vampire disco diva with sky-high feathered golden hair, glitter eyeshadow, wine-dark lipstick over small fangs, a white jumpsuit and a black satin cape gliding on white roller skates, four pale backup skaters in matching gold hot pants and bat-wing capes behind her, a teenager sitting on a bench lacing up rental skates, white sparkles on the dark floor, wide shot

choices.label: Race her lap for lap

success.text: Ten laps, elbows out, the Lovelies hissing on every turn. On the last straightaway you dig in and pass the Countess by a skate length. She skids to a stop in a spray of glitter, gasping, not because she lost, but because she cannot remember the last time anyone gave her a real race. "Again," she says, almost smiling. "Some other night."
success.art: A teenager crossing the finish line on a dark roller rink a skate-length ahead of a vampire diva, glitter spraying from her skidding wheels, backup skaters gasping

failure.text: She laps you twice and pats your head as she passes. When you finally coast off the rink, your reflection in the rail shows a little crease between your eyebrows that was not there yesterday. The Countess, meanwhile, looks radiant.
failure.art: An exhausted teen gripping the rink rail, their reflection showing a new worry line, a radiant vampire diva gliding past with a smug wave

choices.label: Skip the race and challenge her to a dance-off instead

success.text: You do the worm on roller skates. You do a move from a breakdancing video that you have only ever seen once. The Lovelies forget to hiss. The Countess stares, horrified, delighted, and starts copying you. "What on earth is that called?" For one song she is not 1977. She is just dancing. The kids slip out the side door.
success.art: A teenager breakdancing on roller skates under a mirror ball, a vampire diva awkwardly trying to copy the move, backup dancers watching openmouthed, kids sneaking out a side door

failure.text: You trip on your own laces mid-spin and land in a heap. The Countess sighs. "This is why the eighties are a tragedy." The Lovelies circle you, and when you limp home your hair has one stubborn silver strand that will not pull out.
failure.art: A teen sprawled on a rink floor in tangled skate laces, four bat-caped skaters circling under a mirror ball, a vampire diva rolling her eyes

signature.title: You Have to Invite Me In
signature.place: Your front door, Crystal Street, 11 p.m.
signature.text: The doorbell plays the first four notes of a disco song it does not know. On the porch stands a tall woman in a white fur stole, gold platform boots and sunglasses at night, twirling a long-stemmed black rose. "Darling, my Cadavrillac has died on your charming little street. May I use your telephone?" She smiles with a few too many teeth and does not step over the threshold. "Of course," she adds lightly, "you'll have to say the words. House rules. Old-fashioned of me."
signature.art: A suburban front door at eleven at night opening onto a tall glamorous woman on the porch in a white fur stole, gold platform boots and sunglasses, sky-high feathered golden hair, twirling a long-stemmed black rose and smiling with small fangs, standing just outside the doorsill, a teenager in pajamas holding the latched screen door, a long black vintage car with gold tail fins at the curb, yellow porch light, medium shot from inside the hallway

choices.label: Keep the screen door latched and chat with her through it

success.text: You do not say the words. You say, "Tell me about your club." She leans on the porch rail and talks for an hour: the farm kids, the shy boys in borrowed platforms, the drag queens, EVERYBODY IS SOMEBODY UNDER THE BALL. She never notices the time. At the first gray light she gasps, says "Rude!" and is gone in a swirl of fur, and she sounds almost grateful.
success.art: A glamorous woman in a white fur stole leaning on a porch rail talking animatedly to a teenager behind a latched screen door, the sky turning pale gray at the horizon

failure.text: "Darling, you're being tiresome." She hums one bar of a disco song through the screen, and your feet start to tap on their own. You shimmy in the hallway until dawn while she watches from the porch, sipping something red from a thermos, and you wake up with the stiff knees of a forty-year-old.
failure.art: A teenager dancing helplessly in a dim hallway behind a screen door, a glamorous woman in fur watching from the porch with a thermos, gold boots tapping

choices.label: Slam the door and bless the threshold

success.text: Slam. You splash blessed water along the doorsill and on every windowsill in the house. She knocks, then taps at the windows, then sighs dramatically down the chimney. "Fine. FINE. I've been thrown out of better houses than this one." At three in the morning you hear her Cadavrillac finally start, and the horn plays a sulky little tune.
success.art: A teenager splashing holy water along a doorsill inside a dark front hall, a glamorous silhouette in fur pressing her palms against the frosted door glass

failure.text: The bottle slips and shatters on the tile. Through the mail slot comes a long, gloved finger, which beckons. You do not open the door, but you spend the whole night sitting against it while she sings you every number one hit from 1977, in order, with commentary.
failure.art: A long gloved finger with sharp painted nails beckoning through a brass mail slot, a teenager slumped against the inside of the door with shards of a broken bottle on the floor

choices.label: Invite her in for cocoa, on your house rules

success.text: "You can come in. Cape on the hook, boots on the mat, and you have cocoa." To your shock, she obeys. She sits at your kitchen table, cocoa untouched, studying the family photos on the fridge. She lingers on one of your grandmother laughing at her seventieth birthday. "She looks wonderful," the Countess says quietly. "How does she do it?" She leaves before you can answer.
success.art: A glamorous vampire woman sitting at a cozy 1980s kitchen table with an untouched mug of cocoa, gazing at family snapshots on a refrigerator, her fur cape hanging on a hook by the door

failure.text: The second you say "come in," she is already in. The TV switches itself to a disco channel, your mother comes downstairs doing the Hustle in her bathrobe, and the Countess dances your whole family around the living room until sunrise. Everybody wakes up with a backache and a mysterious taste for easy listening.
failure.art: A glamorous vampire woman leading a family in bathrobes in a disco dance around a suburban living room at night, a mirror ball spinning from the ceiling fan

signature.title: Mirror, Mirror at Glamour Snaps
signature.place: Glamour Snaps portrait studio, Starlight Mall, 10 p.m.
signature.text: Glamour Snaps is running a midnight special: LOOK LIKE 1977 AGAIN! A line of kids from school sits in the makeover chairs while pale assistants in gold hot pants feather their hair and dab glitter on their cheeks. Each time the big flash pops, the kid in the chair sags a little, and gets up with crow's feet. You are next in line. In the huge lit makeup mirror you can see yourself, the chairs, the hairdryers and the assistants. You cannot see the woman in the gold jumpsuit standing right behind you, her hand resting on your shoulder.
signature.art: A glitzy mall portrait studio at ten at night, a row of makeover chairs facing a huge mirror ringed with bulbs, high school kids in the chairs getting feathered hair and glitter cheeks from pale assistants in gold hot pants, a big camera flash popping on a tripod, a kid rising from a chair with crow's feet, a teenager seated at the mirror and in the reflection only the empty room behind them, while a gloved hand rests on the teenager's shoulder, bright bulb light, medium shot

choices.label: Spin around and snap her with your own camera

success.text: Flash. The Countess shrieks and covers her face, but the photo is already sliding out. It develops into a woman you do not recognize: silver hair, laugh lines, maybe sixty, gorgeous and laughing at something off camera. The woman she would be now. She snatches it from your hand and stares at it, and forgets to stop the kids from leaving.
success.art: An instant photo developing in a teenager's hand showing a laughing silver-haired woman around sixty, a glamorous vampire in a gold jumpsuit reaching for it with a stunned expression in a portrait studio

failure.text: Flash. The photo comes out showing only you, alone, in front of an empty chair, and two cold hands settle on your shoulders. "Darling, never take a lady's picture without asking." You get the full makeover. Your hair stays feathered for a week and your back is stiff for two days.
failure.art: A teenager in a makeover chair with enormous feathered hair and glitter cheeks, two cold gloved hands on their shoulders, an instant photo on the floor showing the teenager alone in the chair

choices.label: Pull the kids out of the makeover chairs before the next flash

success.text: You grab wrists and haul, chair by chair, glitter flying. The assistants hiss and grab back, but the kids come stumbling out the studio door into the dark mall concourse, young, confused, and furious about their hair. Behind you, the big camera flash pops at an empty chair and shatters.
success.art: A teenager dragging glitter-dusted classmates out of makeover chairs through a portrait studio door into a dark mall concourse, pale assistants in gold hot pants hissing behind them, a camera flash bursting

failure.text: An assistant spins your chair around before you can get up. Pop goes the flash. You stagger out with your friends, all of you rubbing your lower backs, arguing about whether music was better in your day, which for some reason now feels like 1977.
failure.art: A group of teenagers shuffling out of a glitzy portrait studio into a dark mall concourse rubbing their lower backs, glitter on their cheeks, a big camera flash glowing behind them

choices.label: Climb in the chair and demand the most 1986 look possible

success.text: "Teased," you tell the assistant. "Huge. Asymmetrical. Neon. Shoulder pads." Half a can of Aqua-Glow later you look like the cover of a synth-pop single. The Countess steps out from behind the mirror, horrified and fascinated. "What IS this?" she whispers, touching the hair. "Is it allowed?" She spends the rest of the night asking for a side ponytail, and nobody else gets the flash.
success.art: A teenager in a makeover chair with enormous teased asymmetrical neon hair and shoulder pads, a glamorous vampire in a gold jumpsuit staring in fascinated horror and touching the hair

failure.text: The assistant ignores you and gives you the full 1977: center part, feathered wings, gold lamé. The flash pops. Your mother screams when you walk in the door, then asks if you want to borrow her old platforms.
failure.art: A teenager with perfectly feathered 1977 hair and a gold lame shirt standing in a suburban doorway at night, a parent holding up a pair of platform shoes

signature.title: Tapping at the Window
signature.place: Your bedroom window, second floor, 2 a.m.
signature.text: Tap. Tap. Tap. You open your eyes. Outside your second-floor window, floating in the air with her roller skates dangling, is one of the Lacroix Lovelies: pale as milk, gold hot pants, bat-wing cape fluttering, a feathered hairdo that has not moved since 1979. She drags one long nail down the glass with a squeal. "Let me in, honey," she sings. "The party's just getting started. It's always just getting started." Her eyes look very, very tired.
signature.art: A pale young woman with a stiff feathered 1979 hairdo floating outside a second-floor bedroom window at two in the morning, gold hot pants and a fluttering bat-wing cape, white roller skates dangling from her feet, one long nail dragging down the glass, tired eyes, a teenager sitting up in bed inside, white moonlight through the window and dark bedroom, medium shot from inside the room

choices.label: Open the window a crack and ask her what year she thinks it is

success.text: "It's 1979, silly." You tell her it's 1986. You tell her about headphone tape players and music videos on cable and the space shuttle and the price of gas. She drifts closer, listening, her face crumpling. "My mom," she says. "I told her I'd be home by one." Her name is Linda, she says. She floats away toward Main Street, slowly, looking at the houses like she is seeing them for the first time.
success.art: A pale young woman in a bat-wing cape floating outside a bedroom window, her face crumpling with emotion as a teenager talks to her through a cracked-open window, moonlit rooftops behind

failure.text: The second the window cracks, she slips in like smoke and skates figure eights around your bedroom ceiling, upside down, singing. She will not leave. You spend the rest of the night on the couch downstairs while disco thumps through the floor above.
failure.art: A pale young woman in gold hot pants roller skating upside down across a teenager's bedroom ceiling, cape flapping, a teenager fleeing out the bedroom door with a pillow

choices.label: Blast her with your flashlight like a sunrise

success.text: You click the flashlight full in her face. She shrieks and tumbles backward through the air like a kite in a gust, cape flapping, and lands in the Delgados' hedge with a crunch of branches. From the hedge comes a muffled voice: "Not cool." She skates off down the sidewalk, and for once her hair is a mess.
success.art: A flashlight beam blasting out of a bedroom window at night, a caped figure in gold hot pants tumbling backward through the air toward a hedge, roller skates flailing

failure.text: The flashlight flickers and dies. In the dark, the Lovely presses her face to the glass and smiles, and then there are two of them, then four, all along the window ledge, tapping in perfect disco rhythm until the sky goes gray.
failure.art: Four pale young women in bat-wing capes crowded on a second-floor window ledge at night tapping on the glass in unison, a teenager clutching a dead flashlight in bed

choices.label: Draw the curtains, turn up the radio and refuse to answer

success.text: Curtains shut, radio on: KGLM's overnight show, and the DJ is playing the loudest, most aggressively 1986 song in the station's library. The tapping falters. It tries to match the beat and cannot. When you peek at dawn, there is only a single gold sequin stuck to the glass, and the faint smell of hairspray.
success.art: A teenager hunkered in bed with the curtains drawn and a glowing clock radio turned up, a single gold sequin stuck to the outside of the window glass in early dawn light

failure.text: The radio picks up nothing but disco. Every station. The curtains blow open on their own, the window unlatches with a click, and you spend the rest of the night holding it shut with both hands while she skates in slow circles outside, humming.
failure.art: A teenager straining to hold a bedroom window shut with both hands as curtains billow inward, a caped figure in roller skates circling in the moonlight outside

signature.title: Mirror Ball Moon
signature.text: A mirror ball the size of a station wagon rises over the Heartstone like a second moon, scattering light across every lawn on Crystal Street. Every teenager on the block is out in their pajamas, dancing in their yards, and with every song they get a little older. Bea is doing her taxes on the porch. Your best friend has reading glasses on a chain and is telling you to turn that racket down. On top of the ball, cape billowing, the Countess blows you a kiss.
signature.art: A mirror ball the size of a station wagon hanging in the sky over a purple crystal rock on a suburban cul-de-sac at one in the morning, scattering white sparkles across every lawn, teenagers in pajamas dancing in their yards, some of them now in frumpy cardigans and reading glasses, an 11-year-old girl with blonde braids and red glasses frowning over a tax form on a porch, a vampire diva with feathered golden hair and a billowing black cape posing on top of the ball, wide shot

choices.label: Crank a synth-pop mixtape so loud it drowns out her disco

success.text: You set a boombox on the hood of a station wagon and blast the most aggressively 1986 synth-pop you own. The disco warps. The kids stop dancing her way and start dancing your way, jerky, robotic, ridiculous, and young. The Countess clutches her ears. "What is this? Is it a car alarm? Is it music?"
success.art: A boombox on a station wagon hood blasting sound waves across a suburban street, teens doing robotic 1980s dance moves, a vampire diva on a floating mirror ball clutching her ears

failure.text: Your batteries die halfway through the first chorus. In the silence, the disco comes back twice as loud, and you find your foot tapping. Then your hips. You dance until dawn, and in the morning your back hurts in a way that feels personal.
failure.art: A dead boombox with its battery door hanging open on a lawn, a teen helplessly dancing under the light of a giant mirror ball at dawn

choices.label: Climb the Heartstone and soak the mirror ball with holy water

success.text: You scramble up the geode and let fly. The blessed water hits the mirror ball and every tile it touches goes dark, like a disco on a Monday. The Countess shrieks, the ball sinks behind the rooftops, and the kids on the lawns blink and rub their eyes and are fifteen again, extremely confused about the cardigans.
success.art: A teen standing on top of a giant purple geode spraying a squirt gun at a floating mirror ball whose tiles go dark where the water hits, a vampire diva shrieking, teens on lawns blinking awake

failure.text: You slip on the geode's glassy side and slide right back down into a hydrangea. The mirror light finds you there and you start to sway. When it finally sets at dawn, you catch yourself humming along to an easy-listening station, and liking it.
failure.art: A teen tangled in a hydrangea bush at the base of a purple geode, mirror ball light falling across them, a squirt gun lying in the grass

signature.title: The Cadavrillac
signature.text: A long black 1977 Cadavrillac with gold tail fins cruises down Crystal Street at midnight, slow as a parade float, disco thumping from its speakers and a little mirror ball spinning on the dashboard. It stops at every house where a teenager lives. Yours is next. The tinted rear window hums down, and a gloved hand flicks a gold-edged invitation onto your lawn: CLUB LACROIX, ADMIT ONE, DRESS CODE FABULOUS. "Need a ride to the party, darling?" purrs a voice from the dark back seat. "The night is young, and so, for now, are you."
signature.art: A long black 1977 luxury car with gold tail fins cruising slowly down a moonlit suburban cul-de-sac at midnight, a small mirror ball spinning on its dashboard, the tinted rear window rolled down and a gloved hand flicking a gold-edged invitation onto a lawn, a teenager in a jacket standing on the lawn beside a bicycle, white moonlight and red taillights, wide shot from the lawn

choices.label: Tell her you can't, you have a curfew

success.text: "Sorry, ma'am. School night. I have a curfew." A long silence from the back seat, then a delighted, scandalized laugh. "A curfew! Darling, I had one of those once. In 1955." The window hums up, and the Cadavrillac rolls on, skipping the next three houses as if she has suddenly lost her appetite for the evening.
success.art: A teenager in pajamas politely waving off a long black car with gold fins at the curb, a gloved hand fluttering from the rear window, a small mirror ball glinting on the dashboard

failure.text: "A curfew? How quaint." The car door swings open by itself, and disco pours out like warm fog, and you are halfway to the curb before your crew grabs you by the back of the shirt. You wake up humming a song you have never heard.
failure.art: Glittering warm fog and colored disco light pouring from the open door of a long black car at the curb, a dazed teenager drifting toward it, friends grabbing the back of their shirt

choices.label: Plant your feet in the headlights holding two drumsticks in a cross

success.text: You cross two marching-band drumsticks and believe in it with your whole heart, and somehow that is enough. The Countess hisses and shades her eyes behind her sunglasses. "Drumsticks? Darling, really?" The Cadavrillac reverses all the way down Crystal Street, offended, honking the first bar of a disco song in protest.
success.art: A teenager standing in blazing headlights on a suburban street holding two drumsticks crossed, a long black car with gold fins reversing away, a vampire diva in sunglasses shielding her face in the back seat

failure.text: She looks at the drumsticks, then at you. "You have to believe in it, sweetie." A gloved finger flicks one drumstick out of your hand and into the gutter, and the car idles in front of your house until dawn.
failure.art: A gloved hand flicking a drumstick out of a teenager's grip beside a long black car at night, the drumstick spinning into the gutter, disco light glowing behind tinted windows

choices.label: Grab your bike and tail the Cadavrillac to see where it goes

success.text: You keep a block back with your headlight off. The Cadavrillac winds through town picking nobody up, and finally parks in the alley behind the Glitter Box beside a cellar door you never noticed, glowing faintly red at the seams. The Countess steps out, looks up at the old building for a long moment, touches the brick like a face she once loved, and goes down the steps.
success.art: A teenager on a bicycle peeking around a dark alley corner, a long black car parked beside a red-glowing cellar door behind a theater, a vampire diva in a white fur stole touching the old brick wall tenderly

failure.text: You round a corner and the Cadavrillac is waiting for you, idling, the back door open. "Following a lady home? Cheeky." Your bike chain snaps, and you walk it home at three in the morning while the car follows the whole way, playing slow songs.
failure.art: A teenager walking a broken bicycle down a dark suburban street at three in the morning, a long black car with gold fins creeping close behind, a small mirror ball glinting through the windshield

signature.title: Disco Demolition Night
signature.place: The Glimmer Falls High stadium, midnight
signature.text: In 1979 a KGLM shock jock named Rocky Rhodes blew up a crate of disco records on the fifty-yard line while the whole town cheered. Tonight at midnight the stadium lights slam on by themselves, and the bleachers fill with sleepwalking neighbors in pajamas. On the field sits a fresh crate, this one full of 1986 records, and tied to it with a gold lamé sash, sweating in his bathrobe, is Rocky Rhodes himself, forty-eight and balding. The Countess swoops down out of the dark on her bat-wing cape and lands on the crate in gold platforms. "Remember this, Glimmer Falls? You cheered." Every time the crowd cheers now, everyone in it ages a year.
signature.art: A high school football stadium blazing with lights at midnight, bleachers full of sleepwalking townspeople in pajamas, on the fifty-yard line a wooden crate of vinyl records with a sweating balding man in a bathrobe tied to it by a gold lamé sash, and a vampire diva with sky-high feathered golden hair, a black satin cape and gold platform boots landing on top of the crate, a teenager sprinting across the grass, hard white floodlight, wide shot

choices.label: Seize the stadium PA and spin a record with a disco beat under the synths

success.text: You drop the needle on a 1986 dance single, all drum machines and synths, and underneath it, steady as a heartbeat, the four-on-the-floor kick of disco. The Countess freezes on the crate. "That beat," she whispers. "Is that mine?" You tell her disco never died; it grew up, moved to the city clubs and got a drum machine. She sits down on the crate to listen, and the crowd stops aging.
success.art: A teenager dropping a needle on a turntable in a stadium press box, a teen DJ cheering beside them, a vampire diva in gold platforms sitting down on a record crate on the field, listening with wonder under the stadium lights

failure.text: The needle skips, and the PA blares the 1979 crowd chanting DISCO SUCKS. The Countess flinches like she has been slapped, and the whole stadium ages two years in one roar. You wake up with a gray hair, which, thankfully, falls out by lunch.
failure.art: A vampire diva flinching on a record crate under blazing stadium lights, a roaring crowd in the bleachers turning gray at the temples, a teenager in a press box wincing at a skipping turntable

choices.label: Sprint onto the field and untie the shock jock

success.text: You slide in under her cape, rip the lamé sash loose and haul Rocky Rhodes off the crate by his bathrobe belt. He sobs all the way to the end zone. "It was a stunt," he keeps saying. "For ratings. I didn't know anybody's whole life was in those records." Up on the crate the Countess hears him, and for one second she looks less like a vampire and more like someone who has waited seven years for an apology.
success.art: A teenager hauling a sobbing balding man in a bathrobe across a floodlit football field toward the end zone, a torn gold sash trailing, a caped vampire diva on a record crate watching with a startled softened face

failure.text: The sash is knotted with something stronger than lamé. The Countess looks down at you, amused. "Defending him, darling? He wouldn't defend you." With a flick of her cape the stadium lights go out, and it takes you an hour to find your way off the field in the dark.
failure.art: A teenager tugging at a glittering knotted gold sash on a record crate as a vampire diva sweeps her bat-wing cape overhead, stadium floodlights blinking out bank by bank

choices.label: Walk up to the crate and ask her how that night felt

success.text: "What was it like," you ask, "watching that on TV?" The Countess looks down at you for a long moment. "Like watching them bury me while everyone clapped," she says. "I was thirty-nine, darling, forever, and the whole world said my kind of fun was over." She steps off the crate, the stadium lights dim one bank at a time, and the sleepwalkers drift home.
success.art: A vampire diva in a gold jumpsuit stepping down from a record crate to face a teenager on a football field, her expression unguarded and sad, stadium lights dimming bank by bank, sleepwalkers drifting from the bleachers

failure.text: She looks at you a long time, then laughs, bright and brittle. "How did it feel? Darling, I don't feel. I dance." The crowd cheers on cue and ages, and so do you, a little: in the morning your knees creak on the stairs.
failure.art: A vampire diva on a record crate laughing brightly with her head thrown back under stadium lights, a cheering crowd in pajamas aging in the bleachers, a teenager rubbing a stiff knee

signature.title: Main Street, 1979
signature.place: Main Street, Glimmer Falls, 11 p.m. the night before Halloween
signature.text: You turn onto Main Street and it is 1979. Gas is eighty-six cents, a station wagon with wood paneling rolls past, and every shop window glows with platform shoes and lava lamps. At the end of the block Club Lacroix is open, the old Rialto blazing with disco light, and at the velvet rope the Countess, young as ever, is turning someone away: a barrel-chested man of fifty in roller skates and a satin jacket, gray at the temples. "Sal, darling," she says, not unkindly. "You're bad for the look." Behind you, 1979 is spreading down Main Street toward Crystal Street like spilled perfume, and every teenager it touches gets a little older.
signature.art: A small-town main street at eleven at night turned back to 1979, a wood-paneled station wagon rolling past, shop windows glowing with platform shoes and lava lamps, an old movie palace at the end of the block blazing with colored disco lights, and at its velvet rope a vampire diva with feathered golden hair and a white jumpsuit holding up a gloved hand to a barrel-chested man of fifty in roller skates and a satin jacket, a teenager on the sidewalk, warm neon, wide shot

choices.label: Unhook the rope yourself and ask Sal to dance right there on the sidewalk

success.text: "Sal? Want to dance?" He blinks at you, a kid he has never met, then grins and holds out a hand. You roller-boogie right there on the sidewalk to the music leaking through the door, badly and joyfully, and the line outside starts clapping. The Countess watches from the rope with a look you have never seen on her face, like she is remembering what the club was for.
success.art: A teenager and a graying man in roller skates and a satin jacket dancing joyfully on a 1979 sidewalk outside a glowing disco club, a line of partygoers clapping, a vampire diva at the velvet rope watching wistfully

failure.text: Sal shakes his head, eyes wet. "Not tonight, kid. She's right. I'm too old for this." He skates away down 1979 Main Street, and the year spreads another block toward Crystal Street.
failure.art: A graying man in a satin jacket roller skating away alone down a glowing 1979 main street at night, a teenager watching from beside a velvet rope, shop windows shifting to lava lamps around them

choices.label: Find a payphone and dial KGLM in 1986 for a way home

success.text: The payphone takes your dime. You dial the KGLM request line, and after a long hiss of static Mix Bell answers: "KGLM, you're on the air, what year is it where you are?" He plays the loudest song of 1986 down the line, and wherever the music spills out of the receiver, Main Street flickers back: VCRs in the windows, a headphone-stereo ad, this year's gas prices. The 1979 tide stops at the corner.
success.art: A teenager holding a payphone receiver blasting music on a small town main street at night, shop windows flickering from lava lamps back to VCRs and headphone stereos around the booth, a disco club glowing at the far end of the block

failure.text: An operator's voice crackles on: "I'm sorry, the number you have dialed is out of service in this decade." The payphone eats your dime, the sidewalk behind you is turning shag-carpet orange, and you run for home just ahead of it.
failure.art: A teenager sprinting away from a payphone booth down a main street at night, the sidewalk behind them turning into orange shag carpet, 1970s cars and lava lamp windows spreading after them

choices.label: March up to the velvet rope and tell the Countess she's making a mistake

success.text: "Everybody is somebody under the ball," you say, pointing up at the motto painted over her own bar. "You said everybody. You didn't say everybody under forty." The Countess opens her mouth, and closes it, and behind her the mirror ball stutters. For one heartbeat her face wavers, and you glimpse the woman she could have been: a gray streak, laugh lines, waving Sal inside. Then 1979 folds up like a fan, and you are standing on a cold 1986 sidewalk.
success.art: A teenager pointing up at a painted motto over a glowing disco bar, a vampire diva at a velvet rope with her face wavering between youth and a graceful silver-streaked older self, a mirror ball stuttering behind her

failure.text: "Darling," she says, tapping your nose with one gloved finger, "nobody tells me anything at my own door." The bat-winged bouncer lifts you by the collar and sets you down at the very back of the line, behind 1979's entire graduating class.
failure.art: A bat-winged bouncer in a tuxedo lifting a teenager by the collar outside a glowing disco club, a vampire diva at the velvet rope laughing, a long line of 1970s teenagers stretching down the block

finale.title: The Last Song at Club Lacroix
finale.place: The Glitter Box Playhouse, Halloween night
finale.text: Halfway through the Glitter Box Halloween revue, the stage splits open and the playhouse remembers what it used to be. Red velvet rolls over the seats, the mirror ball descends from the fly loft, and the audience is on its feet dancing, aging a year with every chorus. The Countess rises from the DJ booth in a jumpsuit of solid gold sequins, lit from within by everyone else's youth, glowing like 1977. "Darling," she says, raising a goblet, "the party never ends."
finale.art: A small theater on Halloween night turned into a glittering 1977 disco, red velvet rolling over the seats, a giant mirror ball descending from the fly loft, a crowd of costumed revue-goers dancing with graying hair, and rising from a DJ booth in the middle of the stage a radiant vampire diva in a gold sequin jumpsuit and black satin cape with sky-high feathered golden hair, raising a goblet, four teenagers in homemade Halloween costumes pushing to the front, gold glow and white sparkles, wide shot

choices.label: Climb the fly rail and cut the mirror ball down

success.text: You climb the rigging hand over hand, swing at the cable and the mirror ball plummets, bursting on the dance floor into ten thousand silver tiles. Golden light floods out of it and back into the crowd. The Countess screams and comes apart into a flock of sequined bats that pours out the stage door into the night.
success.art: A giant mirror ball shattering on a dance floor in a burst of silver tiles and golden light, a vampire diva dissolving into a flock of sequined bats fleeing out a stage door

failure.text: The cable will not cut. The Countess floats up beside you on the rigging. "Oh, you're sweet," she murmurs, and kisses you on the cheek, and you feel ten years slide out of you like a breath.
failure.art: A vampire diva floating beside a teen clinging to theater rigging, kissing their cheek as golden light flows out of them into her

choices.label: Have Frankie throw the house lights: last call

success.text: "LAST CALL!" you bellow, and every fluorescent work light in the Glitter Box slams on at once. The most dreaded words in nightlife. In the flat white glare, the disco is just a sticky floor and a cheap ball, and the magic drains out of it like flat soda. The Countess shields her eyes and flees, wailing, "Not the house lights! Not the house lights!"
success.art: Harsh white fluorescent work lights blasting on over a glittering disco, revealing a sticky floor and tacky decorations, a vampire diva shielding her face and fleeing, a stage manager at a light board grinning

failure.text: The breaker sparks and the work lights die. In the dark, only the mirror ball keeps spinning, brighter than ever. "Sweetie," says the Countess, "in my club, it is never last call."
failure.art: A sparking breaker box in a dark theater, a mirror ball spinning brighter than ever over dancers, a vampire diva laughing in the spotlight

choices.label: Bring Glory, Zelda and Sal onto the floor and let the last song end

success.text: You put Sal's scratched record on the turntable, Night Fever Forever, and this time you do not stop it. Onto the floor walk three people with gray in their hair and nothing to apologize for: Glory in full drag, Zelda in her best furs, Sal on his roller skates. "Doreen," Zelda calls, "your roots are showing, and you look marvelous." The Countess stares at them, her old friends, older and happier than she has ever let herself be. The needle reaches the scratch, and passes it.
success.alone: You put Sal's scratched record on the turntable, Night Fever Forever, and this time you do not stop it. Onto the floor walk two people with gray in their hair and nothing to apologize for: Zelda in her best furs, Sal on his roller skates. "Doreen," Zelda calls, "your roots are showing, and you look marvelous." The Countess stares at them, her old friends, older and happier than she has ever let herself be. The needle reaches the scratch, and passes it.
success.art: Three joyful older people with gray hair dancing onto a disco floor, a drag queen in sequins, a former scream queen in furs and a silver-haired man on roller skates, holding their hands out to a stunned vampire diva, a record spinning past a scratch on a turntable

failure.text: The record skips at the scratch and jumps back to the chorus, again and again. The Countess laughs, a little too loudly. "See? It never ends. Nothing has to end." She is not ready to look at her friends' faces yet.
failure.art: A turntable needle skipping on a scratched record, a vampire diva laughing too loudly with her back turned to three older friends holding out their hands

choices.label: Keep her talking about her glory days until dawn, the trick that worked that first week

success.text: That first week taught you her weakness: ask the Countess about her club and she forgets the clock. So you step up to the DJ booth and ask. "Tell me about New Year's Eve, 1976. Who was on the floor?" She tells you, goblet waving, about the farm kids and the drag queens and the shy boys in borrowed platforms, and the dancing slows as the whole room listens, while your crew quietly rolls up the Glitter Box loading door on the first gray light of November. The Countess turns mid-sentence, sees the sunrise, shrieks "Rude!" and flees under the stage in a swirl of sequins, and the stolen youth drifts back into the crowd like glitter settling.
success.art: A vampire diva in a gold sequin jumpsuit shrieking and shielding her eyes from pale dawn light pouring through a rolled-up theater loading door, a costumed teenager at the DJ booth grinning, glitter drifting down over the crowd

failure.text: She starts to tell you, then catches herself and laughs. "Oh no, darling. I've fallen for that one before." The music swells, and you feel a whole year slip by in a single chorus.
failure.art: A vampire diva in a gold sequin jumpsuit wagging a gloved finger at a costumed teenager beside a DJ booth, a mirror ball blazing, a crowd dancing faster beneath it

choices.label: Call her out onto her own floor for a dance battle, like you took her on midweek

success.text: Midweek you learned that the Countess cannot resist a challenge on her own turf, whether it is the rink, the studio or the stadium, so you point straight at the DJ booth. "You and me, Countess. Dance floor. Now." The battle is ferocious: her hustle against your moonwalk, her spins against your worm, and every move you throw pulls a year of youth back out of the mirror ball and into the crowd. When you finish on your knees in a full split, the whole Glitter Box screams, and the Countess, breathless and outdanced, throws up her gloved hands, bows once like a star, and retreats under the stage in a storm of sequins.
success.art: A costumed teenager landing a dramatic split on a glowing dance floor under a mirror ball, a breathless vampire diva in gold sequins throwing up her gloved hands in defeat, a cheering crowd ringing the floor

failure.text: She matches every move and adds a spin. The crowd cheers for her, ages a year, and keeps cheering. You leave the floor gasping, but you saw her falter once, on the worm, and she saw you see it.
failure.art: A vampire diva in gold sequins spinning triumphantly on a glowing dance floor, a winded costumed teenager doubled over beside her, a cheering crowd under a blazing mirror ball

choices.label: Unhook the velvet rope for her, like you did for Sal the night before Halloween, and let the song end

success.text: The night before Halloween you watched her turn her own regulars away at the rope, so tonight you unhook a velvet rope from the stage, hold it open for her, and give her own motto back to her. "Everybody is somebody under the ball, Doreen. Even you. Even older." Sal skates through first, then Glory and Zelda, gray and glorious, holding out their hands. She takes them, steps down from the DJ booth and dances with her old friends as the needle reaches the scratch on the record, and passes it, and the last song finally, gorgeously, ends.
success.art: A vampire diva in gold sequins stepping down from a DJ booth to take the hands of three gray-haired friends, a drag queen in full sequins, an older woman in furs and a man on roller skates, a costumed teenager holding open a velvet rope

failure.text: She stares at the open rope, and at her friends' gray hair, and cannot make herself step through. "Not yet," she whispers, and the record skips back to the chorus. She almost did it.
failure.art: A vampire diva in gold sequins frozen at the edge of a DJ booth staring at an open velvet rope held by a costumed teenager, gray-haired friends waiting below, a record spinning on the turntable

best.title: Let the Song End
best.text: The song ends. For the first time since 1980, there is silence on Doreen's dance floor, and then the whole Glitter Box applauds. The golden light flows out of her and back into the crowd, and every year she stole goes back where it came from. The doors open on dawn. Doreen walks into the sunrise, flinches, and does not burn. She just gets older, nine years in nine seconds: a silver streak like a lightning bolt, laugh lines, reading glasses she pretends are a fashion choice. She is forty-eight, and she is gorgeous, and she knows it. The next Saturday, the Glitter Box revue debuts a new act, Countess Doreen, Forever Fabulous, and Disco Tuesday at the roller rink is packed to the rails with every regular Club Lacroix ever had.
best.art: A glamorous woman in her late forties with feathered golden hair, one silver streak, laugh lines and reading glasses stepping out of a small theater into a pink sunrise and laughing, flanked by a tall drag queen in a magenta sequin gown, a 63-year-old woman in a white fur coat and cat-eye glasses, and a barrel-chested man with a silver pompadour on roller skates, teenagers in rumpled Halloween costumes cheering on the sidewalk, warm dawn light, wide shot

good.title: House Lights Up
good.text: The Countess flees into the night, and the youth she stole flows back into the crowd like the bass returning after a skip. Nobody in the audience remembers much except the best dance of their lives. The trapdoor under the Glitter Box stage gets nailed shut. Sometimes, on very slow Tuesday nights, Sal swears he sees a figure in a cape watching the rink from the parking lot.
good.art: A teenager kneeling on an empty theater stage at dawn hammering nails into a square of sparkling floorboards, a scatter of glitter on the boards and a single black sequined feather beside the hammer, gray dawn light from the open loading door, medium shot

bittersweet.title: A Little Gray Around the Edges
bittersweet.text: You end the party, but not before the Countess takes her tithe. A few kids from the revue keep their reading glasses and an inexplicable love of the evening news, and you have a single silver strand in your hair that never goes away. The Countess is sealed back under the stage in her mirrored coffin, still thirty-nine, still 1977, still alone.
bittersweet.art: A teenager leaning close to a bathroom mirror and pinching a single silver strand in their dark hair, and below the bathroom through a cutaway of the floor a theater stage with cracks in the boards and a mirrored coffin glinting under the stage, soft morning light, medium shot

bad.title: Forever 1977
bad.text: Your crew leaves the Glitter Box at dawn, and you do not. They only see you now in reflections: in the mirror ball, in shop windows, in the chrome of Joey's bumper, always dancing in gold hot pants and a bat-wing cape, the newest of the Lacroix Lovelies. You look young. You look happy. You look like you are trying very hard to tell them something over the music.
bad.art: A shop window at dawn whose glass reflects a sparkling disco inside, where a teenager in gold hot pants and a bat-wing cape dances with a strained smile and one hand pressed to the glass, while on the real sidewalk three worried friends in jackets press their hands against the window from outside, pale pink dawn light, medium shot
